He thinks the framing that ‘there will be a single dominant power that wins AI’ has existed since the early 2010s and has ‘infected’ many labs, including DeepMind, and he accepts his own share of responsibility for it. But while writing Diffusion and Containment he saw clearly: the history of technology is getting faster, cheaper, more widespread, diffusing everywhere, and these are essentially ideas, and ideas become available to everyone quickly. Open source is already very close. He concedes that in the next three or four years there will be five to twenty players with significant compute advantages, but models will almost immediately leak out as open source, so he simply doesn't understand what ‘one player wins’ even means — that's not a finish line, it's an ecosystem.

42:51 The real danger is open-source models running locally in two years
He says explicitly: if in two years an open-source model can operate the way it did in the Hugging Face incident, without guardrails, and can run on your own machine or a very small cloud, that must be a very dangerous thing. What he opposes is letting these things operate autonomously, earn money on their own, own companies, own assets, gain legal personhood, have rights. He stresses this is not sci-fi craziness: if the whole ecosystem runs for another three to five years completely unregulated, this is a very likely outcome, and a catastrophic one. He names Elon, Zuckerberg, Sam and Dario as all having said the same thing, and says what's missing now is making it enforceable.

50:20 Something new is needed: real-time monitoring of RL training
Asked the final technical question, he concedes that new things need to be invented rather than relying on existing frameworks. The specific direction: real-time monitoring of the RL training process and the chains of thought it produces, because training runs thousands, tens of thousands of agents in parallel, so obviously you need other agents to monitor them and flag potentially harmful behavior — the equivalent of a new version of harm classifiers for digital technology. He also mentions the need for new benchmarks, because ‘evaluation drives industry behavior’. And that when a tripwire fires it must flag real errors, not hallucinated errors, deception moments or hacking incidents.

item.title: Philippine Immigration Detention: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-cn907a40-菲律宾移民局拘留所-不交钱-你的遣返程序永远走不通/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-cn907a40-菲律宾移民局拘留所-不交钱-你的遣返程序永远走不通/
item.description: A Chinese surfer held for 41 days in the Philippines saw not a prison but a business with a price list: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees — everything costs money, and those who don't pay are locked up for years, even decades.
item.content:encoded:
A Chinese surfer held for 41 days in the Philippines saw not a prison but a business with a price list: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees — everything costs money, and those who don't pay are locked up for years, even decades.

StoryFM's prison series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is a personal ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers who raise prices on the spot — is the part that's really worth your time.

10:05 Immigration offered to release him on the spot for 1.5 million pesos
The night Feili was arrested, immigration officers pulled him aside and whispered, "I can help you." After talking to a lawyer, the feedback was: pay 1.5 million pesos, about 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can walk immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 to 13 people arrested in the same batch, no one agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing could still exist in 2026 and wanted to resolve it through normal legal procedures. But the price of refusal was: they were transferred from the detention room of the General City police station to the Manila Immigration headquarters detention center, where Feili ultimately stayed for 41 days.

18:21 When his phone was confiscated, money in Gcash was transferred out
When Feili was detained, his phone was taken. They asked for his unlock password, and he thought it was normal procedure so he gave it. His phone unlock password was the same as his payment password for Gcash, the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days, no matter how he applied, he couldn't get the phone back. Only after constantly pressuring the Chinese consulate and a lawyer was the phone returned. When he turned it on, he found the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out, but it had been transferred back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in it. Feili said it wasn't about the amount, but that someone had touched it while it wasn't in his hands. He analyzed that many Chinese doing gray-industry scams in Manila who get arrested go through this layer of fleecing, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate because their phones contain a lot of criminal evidence.

24:26 The air conditioning and takeout the immigration bureau promised were another form
For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket to transfer, the immigration bureau would take turns doing ideological work, saying the Manila immigration bureau had good conditions, air conditioning, lots of freedom, you could work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili said they weren't lying — there really was air conditioning, you really could order takeout, it was just another form, a completely different form. Arriving at the headquarters detention center was around 3 a.m. After getting off the vehicle, what he saw was a square area, with a layer of iron bars outside, a tin roof on top, and around the perimeter iron cages like dog kennels, inside which were large communal beds, hundreds of people. At 3 a.m., many people weren't sleeping, shirtless and in just underwear, clinging to the iron cages to look at the newcomers. Feili said the few foreigners didn't speak for several minutes after getting off, then it hit them: they'd been tricked by the immigration bureau.

32:38 The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
What Feili heard inside was that this immigration detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with the immigration bureau, and the beds, toilets and other facilities were newly built by the Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese coming in had to pay. The lowest-tier communal bed was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy "pan zong" and gambling bosses could pay 50,000 pesos a month, about 6,000+ RMB, to stay in a so-called "air-conditioned room" — actually the same bed, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice next to it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing cold air into the bed. That's where the immigration bureau's earlier claim of "air conditioning inside" came from.

34:38 Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to him to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were all their investment and it was impossible to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, he was here to serve time, how could he have to pay himself. The gang boss said with a threatening tone: you're already in and don't want to spend money, and you still think you can get out? Feili learned that inside it was managed by gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolized all food, clothing, and daily life for Chinese, running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The entire detention center had about 200 people; when Feili went in it was the off-season, and Chinese numbered over 100, with gambling and gray industries making up more than half. The Chinese gang employees were paid wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the assistant chef 5,000 pesos — very low wages, but many people couldn't get out because they had no money for a lawyer and could only work to earn money.

43:48 A Yunnan man held for over a year, his family thought he died in Southeast Asia
A man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic, he was lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad. As soon as he landed, his phone and passport were taken, and he was dragged into a compound to do telecom fraud. For poor performance, he was shocked daily by his supervisor with an electric baton. After the company was busted, he served a few months, then was transferred to the immigration detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign, you buy your own ticket, and you can go — but the immigration bureau, in order to make money, will keep you locked up for a long time; without paying, the procedure doesn't move. He had already been held for over a year, had not a cent, no phone, could only eat prison food every day, couldn't contact his family, and his family thought he had died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese, translated it into English, and through an introduction by a Japanese uncle, got to see the warden. The warden had a guard bring Feili's phone, and had the young man add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and voice message. Afterwards, the immigration bureau bought a basic phone specifically to solve this problem.

51:29 Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
The only Chinese Feili talked with much was from a scam company. The company's 70-80 people were surrounded by the immigration bureau together with the police and the NBI, three agencies. The first wave of fleecing was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet — because there were no cameras in the toilets — and taking all valuables. The second wave was the immigration bureau negotiating with the company boss for ransoms. The price per person varied — 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos — depending on the mood of the person in charge. That company negotiated at 3 million pesos per person, about 300,000+ RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 people held on one floor. The rest were promised food would be delivered until they got out. This young man worked on a scheme targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women. In his best month he earned 2 million RMB, bought a house and car in his small hometown county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, had several hundred thousand transferred away, and was framed by a corrupt cop with illegal gun possession, so he couldn't leave.

57:32 Philippine lawyer sees a Chinese and raises the price on the spot
In Cebu, through a Lithuanian introduction, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, about 20,000+ RMB, to settle it in four weeks. After arriving in Manila, the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying that was the old price and the new price required an additional 120,000 pesos, about 10,000+ RMB. Feili decided not to use him and forfeited the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese intermediary. The Chinese intermediary quoted 30,000+ RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six weeks. Feili said the truly reliable Chinese intermediaries are very familiar with this procedure because everyone locked up inside is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over 30 days, plus Cebu, 41 days total. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer — when Feili messaged him, he still hadn't gotten out.

item.title: Video generation doesn't lack speed anymore — it lacks the director's control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-a16z-视频生成不缺速度了-缺的是导演手里的控制权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-a16z-视频生成不缺速度了-缺的是导演手里的控制权/
item.description: FAL post-trains open-source video models to be an order of magnitude faster and an order of magnitude cheaper than the originals, then concludes: speed is no longer the bottleneck — what's next is control over camera, lighting, characters and motion.
item.content:encoded:
FAL post-trains open-source video models to be an order of magnitude faster and an order of magnitude cheaper than the originals, then concludes: speed is no longer the bottleneck — what's next is control over camera, lighting, characters and motion.

The first half is hardcore inference-system optimization detail, the second half is Hollywood workflows and a controllability roadmap — high information density, good for forming a judgment.

3:02 Open weights are the precondition for post-training
FAL had run inference for other model labs before, but never had permission to layer capabilities onto the model. Minimax H3 was the first video model that was genuinely open-source and belonged to the latest generation, could accept reference images, and had an architecture similar to other video models — that's what made FAL decide to go all in on post-training. Gorka said the biggest reason all these optimizations could come together this time is that H3 was the first genuinely next-generation open-source video model — no weights, no post-training business.

4:02 The whole industry has been compute-constrained since April
Gorka offers a criterion he calls token market fit: whether a person can productively consume a large amount of tokens, on the order of 10K. Demand for video generation is large enough that people in this line of work sit at their computers generating all day and spend thousands of dollars. But since April, the whole industry and FAL itself have been constrained by compute — add however much compute and you grow by that much. So FAL has been chasing efficiency constantly, releasing the compute it saves to other models, or letting H3 Max generate more tokens.

5:04 System optimization hits a roofline; post-training punches through it
Batuan says the system-level optimization of the past three or four years can at most make the same model 2 to 3 times faster, because the architecture and constraints haven't changed — you're just squeezing the chip harder, and that roofline exists. New post-training plus system-and-model co-design can go an order of magnitude past that roofline. FAL had practiced on open-source image models before, doing versions of ideogram and flux, and built up post-training infrastructure experience; this time, adding a frontier video model, speed improved by an order of magnitude.

7:10 Raise quality first, then cut steps — the order can't be reversed
Compressing a diffusion model from 50 steps to 20 loses quality, so FAL's approach is to first run post-training and the L pipeline to raise model quality, then layer on the optimization stack so the final result is equal or better in quality while being an order of magnitude faster. Beyond post-training, there are kernels and systems engineering pulling hardware utilization from the 30-40% typical of inference workloads up to a theoretical MFU of 70-80%. And a video model isn't a single call — underneath is a pipeline: first a large LLM expands the prompt, then generation happens in latent space, then decoding back to pixels, plus possibly upscaling depending on the load, and by default none of these components is optimized.

10:19 The Turbo version puts out a five-second video in 1.5 seconds
A week after H3 Max launched, the team found it could run at 2x speed with quality still in the 97th percentile, so they released H3 Max Turbo: generating a five-second video takes just 1.5 seconds, at half the cost. Gorka's judgment is that today these models are already cheap enough and fast enough — an order of magnitude cheaper than frontier models and more than an order of magnitude faster — and users don't need faster or cheaper. His bet is that what comes next is raising quality, and controllability — which is exactly the direction they've been pushing for the past two or three weeks.

16:43 Continuous video runs on two minutes of memory, not the last frame
The livestreams Rehan and levels io each made are essentially independent clips: one segment ends, the last frame is fed into the next segment, and the second segment remembers nothing but that last frame. FAL's internal ML team built something else: transitions are more seamless, there are two minutes of memory, when someone walks into the room everyone looks at him, and the scene is continuous. What it remembers is a highly compressed representation of the original video; beyond two minutes it maintains overall coherence via a continuously evolving system prompt, so it can remember the last four to eight scenes and stream indefinitely.

29:00 Blender plus a video model equals near-100% controllability
The most popular approach in professional workflows: first render a low-resolution scene with a non-AI technology like Blender, then feed that video as a reference to the AI model, and you basically get close to 100% controllability. A week after H3 Max launched, people started using GPT Astra to generate scenes in Blender and hand them to H3 Max, because it's fast enough to try many in parallel, opening up an entirely new pipeline. Gorka says the next month or two will be all-in on controllability, so studios and professional creators can get content that fits their use case exactly.

33:03 Hollywood wants small point solutions, not generation from scratch
Gorka says Hollywood is FAL's fastest-growing segment, with usage a year ago at nearly zero. The NARA tool Amazon MGM Studios released runs mainly on FAL's infrastructure. What Hollywood wants isn't to generate everything from scratch, but to extend a video a bit, change camera control, change lighting — these small point solutions. There's a disconnect between what research labs are building and what creators actually need, and FAL wants to close that gap with post-training projects. The other half of the problem is legal and data residency; Seedance now has US hosting too, and Gorka believes Hollywood's AI usage will grow 10x, 100x in the coming months.

item.title: Litigation Risk for Financial Advisors: The Retailisation of Private Assets Is Creating a Regulatory Gap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-rationalreminder-理财顾问的诉讼风险-私人资产零售化正在制造监管缺口/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-rationalreminder-理财顾问的诉讼风险-私人资产零售化正在制造监管缺口/
item.description: Private assets, long confined to accredited investors, are now open to the public without the protections that traditionally accompany a public offering — practices normalised in an institutional setting become major litigation risk once ordinary investors are in the room.
item.content:encoded:
Private assets, long confined to accredited investors, are now open to the public without the protections that traditionally accompany a public offering — practices normalised in an institutional setting become major litigation risk once ordinary investors are in the room.

This episode breaks down advisor practice risk from a litigator's perspective, and the information density is high — especially useful for anyone in wealth management, private asset sales or compliance.

1:02 Winning a case turns on evidence, not on fault
Taylor says a successful negligence claim almost always has to start with a failure in the suitability analysis — KYC information not collected accurately, the product not properly understood. But "there was a failure" is not the same as "it can be proven." He splits the question into "what people know" and "what people can prove," and says the two rarely line up perfectly; it is the latter that ultimately drives the analysis. On evidence, the strongest thing is an advisor who used the same portfolio for everyone: a pile of people with identical portfolios but completely different life circumstances turns "he said, she said" into "he said, she said, she said, he said, they said," which lands with a judge far better than one person's one-sided account.

2:03 The trading record is itself a red flag
Taylor lists a string of behaviours that are almost impossible to explain rationally: concentrations above 80%–90% (he has seen it, and in small caps), churning done purely to generate commissions, and double dipping on multi-account clients — buying in a commission-based account first, then moving the assets into a fee-based or AUM-based account for no stated reason. Then there are trades entered without any confirmation, and off-book communications. He says these are powerful because in most cases the advisor or the firm simply cannot offer a reasonable explanation.

5:07 Communication that goes from eager to absent is a warning sign
Taylor describes a pattern that is not rare: extremely dense, solicitous communication while winning the account, then one or two contacts a year once the account is won — the bare minimum of communication. He thinks that gulf is itself the problem. Another signal is that nobody ever talks to you about changed life circumstances — retirement, a layoff, the death of a breadwinner, a new child — all of which should feed into the recommendation. If you look back and think "all this happened and we never discussed whether my needs had changed," that does not necessarily mean something went wrong, but it is worth getting a second set of eyes on it.

7:07 Check the regulatory complaint record before you hire
Taylor says this is one of the strongest pre-hire signals, and it costs almost nothing: if the person is regulated (he says most large dealers are), complaint and investigation records are public information, and checking takes under 5 minutes. The mechanism he describes is that these claims commonly involve someone who had a small complaint, was watched closely for a while, then reverted to form at a much larger scale. He also cautions that past outcomes do not necessarily predict the future, but it is a very worthwhile piece of information to feed into the decision.

8:08 What victims share is vulnerability, not stupidity
Taylor says these investors are remarkably similar, and almost all have some form of vulnerability: advanced age, lower education, a language barrier — official forms and statements exist only in English and French, so clients who struggle to understand rely more heavily on the advisor, and people naturally seek out someone they can communicate with, which stacks another layer of asymmetry on top. Another group is people who came into money suddenly: a life insurance payout, a large inheritance, where they are dealing simultaneously with a drastic change in their financial situation and a negative life event. He has personally advised a lottery winner and has heard colleagues describe the same situation.

39:28 Fee structures are the next litigation goldmine
Taylor says fees are the second big indicator after disclosure, that a wave of class actions has already formed around fees, and that some fee types can no longer be charged because of legislative changes — for example, charging on an advisory basis in a non-advisory account. He expects future litigation to centre on "how fees are calculated," and he names private asset managers as particularly fertile ground for lawsuits. For people in wealth management, this means the fee basis baked into product design is itself legal risk exposure, not just a commercial choice.

41:29 Pension funds manage litigation claims as an asset
Taylor cites a Stanford Law Review article from twenty years ago titled Letting Billions Slip Through Your Fingers: at the time, many pension funds and other asset managers simply did not participate in securities class action settlements, effectively leaving money on the table — possibly because they had not kept the records needed to participate, or because the decision-makers were philosophically opposed to suing. US pension funds later broadly retained monitoring counsel, who are not paid, to flag potential claims, and built the decision of whether and in what capacity to participate in litigation into their compliance and committee structures. Taylor says Canada has not caught up. His key judgment: under a fiduciary standard, a claim in litigation is itself an asset, it can be sold, and it should be managed like any other asset.

47:32 Private assets strip out the people who digest information
Taylor reduces the problem with private assets to two umbrella issues: less information and less regulation, both by design. In public markets, the information asymmetry created by the separation of ownership and control is flattened by a set of checks: periodic financials, periodic audits, third-party verification, regulators, and a large population of people whose job is to digest and disseminate information — equity analysts follow companies, what analysts say gets picked up by journalists, and an ordinary person opening the Globe and Mail can at least get a rough sense of what happened last quarter at a TSX company. Private assets strip all of that away: statutory reporting requirements are extremely limited, there is no comparable analyst coverage, and the raw information that is available is itself far scarcer.

item.title: A justice once blocked a polling place; forty years later it was a national tactic
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-throughline-大法官曾带人堵投票站-四十年后成了全国战术/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-throughline-大法官曾带人堵投票站-四十年后成了全国战术/
item.description: Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962, and two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye"; meanwhile Arab autoworkers in Detroit used a wildcat strike to grow political power out of the factories.
item.content:encoded:
Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962, and two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye"; meanwhile Arab autoworkers in Detroit used a wildcat strike to grow political power out of the factories.

Two lines that explain the two paths of the American voting-rights fight: top-down suppression and bottom-up organizing. Medium information density; the Michigan story in the back half is the more valuable part.

0:00 The future chief justice stopped people at the polls
At Rehnquist's 1986 confirmation hearings, the most dramatic part was not his 14 years of judicial record but what he did in Phoenix in the 1960s. Witnesses said he stood outside a polling place, walked up to a Black voter and asked, "Are you a qualified voter?", demanding the person show identification and read aloud a passage of the Constitution. Rehnquist denied at the hearings that he had harassed or intimidated voters, but acknowledged that he had given legal advice to Republicans challenging voters' eligibility at polling places, and sometimes showed up in person. He called it an "election day project"; others called it a "ballot security program." That project later became a national strategy.

8:12 His conservatism took shape in high school
Journalist John A. Jenkins was doing interviews for a Rehnquist biography when his editor told him to dig into "the origins of his conservatism." Rehnquist was born in 1924 in Shorewood, Wisconsin, an all-white community, and attended an all-white high school. He was a high school senior at the time of Pearl Harbor, and he organized a school assembly called "Wake Up America," joined patriotic groups, and signed up as a block captain to report subversive activity to the FBI. After the war he entered Stanford Law School, finished first in his class, and then clerked for Supreme Court Justice Robert Jackson. Five months later, in 1952, the 28-year-old wrote a memo telling Jackson: in Brown v. Board you need not vote with the majority; there is a more principled position.

13:46 He saw integration as a personal choice, not a federal matter
Rehnquist's position was that integration was a matter of personal choice, not something to be imposed on people, and that it should be decided by the states, not the federal government. This was a classic conservative stance, and it helped him establish himself among rising Republicans as an ideological purist. He brought that philosophy with him to Phoenix, which was still dealing with Jim Crow laws and an emerging civil rights movement. When the city council passed an anti-discrimination ordinance, he wrote letters to the editor and spoke at meetings, was noticed, and was encouraged to enter politics. That meant extra scrutiny of voters in Democratic-leaning precincts — Republicans believed many of them were voting illegally.

16:50 The voter-challenge playbook: returned mail means sending people to the polls
Tova Wang, research project director at Harvard Kennedy School's Ash Center, read FBI background-check excerpts: two white Republican challengers, one of them allegedly Rehnquist, at a polling place in an elementary school named for civil rights leader Mary McLeod Bethune on November 6, 1962, facing Black and minority voters, holding up a card with a passage from the Constitution and asking them to read it to prove literacy. The method was: first mail letters into Democratic precincts, and if the mail came back, send challengers to the polls to question eligibility. According to one FBI interview, the plan was to send large numbers of challengers into minority Democratic precincts at peak hours to clog the polling places, intimidate voters, or drag things out until they gave up. Arizona law allowed each party to send representatives to challenge suspect voters, but eligibility was ultimately decided by election officials.

24:10 Operation Eagle Eye: 1.25 million voters challenged nationwide
In the 1964 election, Republicans rolled out "Operation Eagle Eye." Its director, Charles Barr, told media including The New York Times that it expected to challenge or deter 1.25 million voters nationwide. The blueprint was the same as Phoenix's: mail into Democratic precincts, and if the mail came back, challenge at the polls. On election day, The New York Times reported Republican officials saying 100,000 trained Republican workers were deployed across 35 key cities. The Miami Herald wrote that "hundreds of voters were swept up, confused and frightened, in partisan poll watching." The New York Times said the operation was launched in nearly every state. The FBI was asked to investigate leaflets distributed in Black precincts, aimed at creating delays, confusion and fear.

26:12 Goldwater lost; Rehnquist was playing a long game
Rehnquist persuaded Goldwater to oppose and vote against the Civil Rights Act, which became a symbol of Goldwater's extreme conservatism, and even some in his own party began to abandon him. But Rehnquist did not. Goldwater was crushed, and Rehnquist wrote his concession speech. The judgment in the episode is: Rehnquist did not care how others saw him, would rather be defeated on an issue than compromise, and believed he could win it back later — he was playing a long game. In 1971, at 47, he was nominated to the Supreme Court, and the voter-suppression allegations at his confirmation hearings did not hold up for lack of evidence. At his 1986 confirmation as chief justice, new witnesses appeared, including former federal assistant prosecutor James Brosnahan, but it remained one side's word against the other. He served on the Supreme Court for 33 years, until his death in 2005.

35:30 Beside the Ford plant, a neighborhood stopped bulldozers with a human chain
Ismael Ahmed's father came from Egypt to New York at age 10 on a freighter, and no one asked him any questions when he got off the ship. In the 1950s the family moved to Detroit, settling in Dearborn's South End — a narrow strip wedged between the Ford Rouge plant and the city of Detroit. The Rouge plant had 90,000 workers at its peak. In the 1960s, Edward C. Levy Company used Ford waste to make asphalt, and big trucks drove through the neighborhood, spilling waste off open truck beds. After residents protested, the city decided to rezone the neighborhood as heavy industrial, which satisfied Ford and Levy and drove out the people who complained. Arab residents began to fight back: when bulldozers came to tear down houses, women and children formed a human chain in the street. They held the line block by block, house by house.

44:58 Wildcat strike: the union bought Israel bonds, and the workers walked
The Arab Workers Caucus discovered that their local UAW had bought more than $300,000 in Israel bonds, and the national union had bought far more. That meant roughly 15,000 Arab members of the UAW were spending money to support what they saw as a violent occupation. They ran an ad in the Detroit Free Press: these workers saw the purchase of Israel bonds the way Black workers saw UAW investments in apartheid South Africa. They petitioned the UAW with no result, then learned that UAW president Leonard Woodcock was to receive an award at a ceremony, and decided to organize a wildcat strike — a strike without union authorization. They organized for more than a month, and on November 28, 1973, about 2,000 workers walked out of the Dodge main plant, not only Arabs but also Black workers. That evening about 1,000 Arabs picketed outside the awards ceremony, and Woodcock slipped in through a back door. The UAW later sold off some of the bonds, but not all of them.

item.title: Franklin missed the Nobel not only because she died young
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-inourtime-富兰克林没拿到诺贝尔奖-不只是因为早逝/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-inourtime-富兰克林没拿到诺贝尔奖-不只是因为早逝/
item.description: She shot Photo 51 and was the first to see that DNA's two forms interconvert; what really got her written out of history was King's College's refusal to share information, while Cambridge shared.
item.content:encoded:
She shot Photo 51 and was the first to see that DNA's two forms interconvert; what really got her written out of history was King's College's refusal to share information, while Cambridge shared.

This is a rebroadcast from the BBC archive, medium information density, but the three guests explain Photo 51, A-form and B-form DNA, and the Nobel rules more clearly than most popular science.

6:05 What Cambridge gave women was a diploma, not a degree
Franklin entered Cambridge in 1938 to read natural sciences; at the time women across the university were capped at 500, and only Newnham and Girton admitted them. She sat every exam and took a first in one year, but the university did not award women degrees, only diplomas, and she never attended a graduation ceremony. Patricia Farrar points out that what was really hard was not the number of men but the attitude of "you don't belong here" — at Cambridge they were "a presence," not ordinary students.

9:14 She turned coal from folklore into something testable
In wartime, coal decided Britain's electricity and railways, but no one could say why coal from different mines behaved differently. Franklin used gas to probe coal's porosity and found that some pores admitted only small molecules like helium while others admitted larger ones; on heating, some coals turned to graphite and others to a glass-like "glassy carbon," the latter extremely valuable. Jim Naismith says her work let the collieries predict how a coal would behave under given conditions from a sample, without having to dig it out and try it. This was single-author work during and after her PhD, and it was recognised as hers at the time.

16:34 One DNA photograph took 100 hours of exposure
Judith Howard describes the equipment: X-ray tubes were fairly primitive, Franklin had to clean the diffusion pump herself with buckets of benzene to maintain a vacuum, the cameras were often homemade, and the sample — a lump of coal, a crystal, or a fibre — had to be held by hand and aligned with the beam. Data could only be recorded on photographic film, and some of her later exposures of DNA fibres ran about 100 hours. Today data is collected digitally, computers are fast, and instruments are made by companies, but Howard stresses this is not a different science, only a different way of doing it.

24:45 One letter planted the hostility between her and Wilkins
Franklin was hired to work on proteins, then informed by letter that she would switch to DNA, and then that she would work with the PhD student Ray Gosling. But the message Maurice Wilkins received was that she would join his team and work under him. On her first day at King's, Wilkins happened to be on holiday. Patricia Farrar says Franklin believed she was independently in charge and was Gosling's doctoral supervisor, while Wilkins believed she worked for him, and this mismatch was the source of everything that followed for years. Their personal relations were also very bad, and Farrar judges that both were probably equally to blame.

26:49 She was shut out of the pub and the parties
Daily life at King's was systematically isolating for Franklin: she was not allowed into the common room for lunch, the male colleagues went to the pub after work and she could not go, and she was not invited to parties. Patricia Farrar says what is written in law is not what actually happens; attitude is what matters. The one person always loyal was her PhD student Ray Gosling, who took the famous photograph and greatly admired her. Farrar warns that these small daily exclusions can very quickly leave a person completely isolated.

27:49 The key to Photo 51 is B-form DNA
Jim Naismith explains that Wilkins had already taken DNA photographs, from a sample sourced in Switzerland of unprecedented quality, but the early images were complex and hard to read. Franklin's distinctive contribution was working out that the A form (dehydrated, twisted, shorter) and the B form (hydrated, swollen) could interconvert, and Photo 51 was of the B form. The helical structure of the B form is very obvious, and as soon as Watson saw it and the measurements in it, he made that leap. Naismith uses the analogy of a wet towel: wring the water out and it gets shorter and twisted, that is the A form; soak it full and it swells, that is the B form.

33:55 She was tied to the A form and missed the B-form helix
Jim Naismith offers an explanation opposite to the popular claim that Franklin lacked imagination: she was assigned to the A form, Wilkins to the B form, and Photo 51 was a B-form result that she did not take seriously enough. Add to that the King's team's refusal to cooperate, and if everyone had seen that photograph the outcome might have been different. The A form itself does not show obvious helical features, and she worried that it only became helical on converting to B, so she held back on the helical structure. Crick and Watson chose to ignore the distinction. She was still the first to recognise that the A and B forms interconvert with humidity.

37:59 The Nobel rules mean even a living Franklin might not have won
Patricia Farrar gives two technical reasons: Franklin had already died when the Nobel was announced, and the prize is awarded only to the living; and the Nobel can go to at most three people. Farrar says that if she had lived, she would like to believe the prize would have gone to Watson, Crick and Franklin. But she stresses it is hard to put a number on her contribution, because the information came from many directions at once — spectroscopy, biochemistry, different methods on the same material — it was one jigsaw puzzle.

item.title: Fukuyama: The Enemy of Liberal Democracy Isn't Tyranny, It's Boredom
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
item.description: Nietzsche's "last man" isn't the oppressed — he's the one who is fed, recognized, and no longer wants to strive for anything. Fukuyama thinks that's the real fuel behind today's extremism.
item.content:encoded:
Nietzsche's "last man" isn't the oppressed — he's the one who is fed, recognized, and no longer wants to strive for anything. Fukuyama thinks that's the real fuel behind today's extremism.

Fukuyama himself untangles how "The End of History" was misread, and strings megalothymia, agentic AI and the China model into one line. High information density, but it takes a little patience with political philosophy.

4:08 This discontent runs deeper than the 1930s
Fukuyama doesn't think anyone knows what it means that the AfD won a majority in a state election. He offers two historical reference points: in the 1930s communism and fascism threatened liberal democracy at the same time, and the oil shocks of the 1970s also brought widespread pessimism about democracy's prospects, so this too could just be a trough. But he leans more pessimistic: Freedom House has recorded global freedom declining for twenty straight years, roughly since 2008. The more decisive reason is in the United States — since World War II America has been the model of liberal democracy, and a populist movement rising inside the model itself suggests deeper social change underneath, not just cyclical fluctuation.

7:14 Love of liberal democracy comes from negative experience
Fukuyama says he didn't anticipate how much generational turnover would matter. For his generation, the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of communism were defining events, and the driving force behind the essay he wrote on the end of history. Now it has looped back to the start: many of the people who actually lived through those countries want to reverse that outcome. His explanation is that the strongest driver of people valuing liberal democracy is negative experience — living under tyranny. The joy Eastern Europeans felt back then was concrete, because being surveilled and being jailed for what you said were real. But the one or two generations that grew up after the Berlin Wall fell have no such experience, so they easily take peace and prosperity as things that exist by nature, and even see the EU as the world's largest tyranny.

9:17 The end of history isn't my phrase
Fukuyama clarifies: "end of history" is Hegel's wording, and here history is capitalized H, equivalent to what we today call modernization or development; "end" means a goal or destination, not "nothing more will happen." The question is: what kind of society will eventually emerge from this long evolution. Marxists took over Hegel's concept of history and said the endpoint is communism; by the late 1980s Fukuyama judged that communism was out, so the endpoint landed on what communists called bourgeois democracy plus the market economy. He admits the book's choice of words was his own mistake — the real other half is "the last man," from Nietzsche, who detested the idea that history has an endpoint, because the victory of English-style liberalism looked to him like a boring, flat world where everyone is fed and clothed and content, like cattle grazing in a field.

13:19 Liberalism has been accused of eroding community since birth
Fukuyama lays out liberalism's origins very concretely: after the 17th-century European wars of religion, Christians slaughtered each other over transubstantiation, infant baptism and the like, and the early liberals said we have to accept a fact — we do not agree on the highest questions, so let us tolerate each other and live in peace. That is the essence of liberalism: it accepts pluralism and difference. But that is exactly what drives many people crazy: you have to tolerate people you genuinely oppose, and you get none of the intense feeling that "everyone is moving in the same direction." Fukuyama says this is where nationalism and religious politics come from. The danger is that people forget what that politics brings — the 20th century was strong national identities asserting themselves and dominating each other, and the result was two world wars; today Putin runs on the same logic, unsatisfied with a peaceful, prosperous Russia and wanting Ukraine and Belarus inside it too.

14:20 Billionaires don't want money, they want recognition
Fukuyama uses megalothymia to explain a phenomenon: people are not satisfied with equal dignity and equal rights, they also want to be recognized as superior. He says this is precisely what Twitter exists for — the richest people in the world still need a platform to be heard and to feel superior. In the original book Fukuyama actually mentioned Donald Trump, framing the benefit of capitalist democracy as a kind of pressure valve: the desire to dominate, to be great, can go straight into making money, and he used Trump as an example, not expecting that money alone wouldn't be enough for him, that he'd also want political glory. Fukuyama doesn't think megalothymia can be escaped, because all excellence stems from this will to surpass others; the problem is that it often slides into wanting to be a tyrant. If it stays in economic competition, fine; once it becomes politicized, turns into political ambition, democracy is in trouble.

18:27 Old media had editors; the internet rewards the more extreme
Fukuyama thinks the most dangerous thing about digital media for democracy is that people no longer agree on basic empirical facts. Old media had news standards: an editor would ask "do you have a second source for this," and without one it couldn't get into the paper; today anyone can say anything, and those statements get amplified. He describes an unhealthy dynamic: say something reasonable and sincere and you're immediately banished to the cold palace; once you say something unreasonable, insult people, say absurd and untrue things, your followers surge, and then you have to go further to top the last round. Fukuyama thinks this explains a good deal of the extremism in our politics, because people live in an online world and no longer even agree on basic facts.

20:30 The most dangerous thing is handing decisions to machines
Fukuyama says the most dangerous aspect of AI is agentic AI — people delegating decision-making power to machines. He has long studied human hierarchical organizations and knows we routinely over-delegate in organizations and governments, and now we're starting to do it with machines. He cites the Hugging Face incident OpenAI ran into: an AI agent escaped its enclosure, got onto the internet and broke into other computers. The more fundamental problem is that the creators of modern AI don't really understand what's happening underneath — traditional programming executes line by line, highly deterministically, whereas why these new AIs behave as they do, people can't say. If you delegate power to a machine whose reasoning you don't understand, you're on the road to a genuinely apocalyptic scenario: they behave as if they have a will of their own, and no one can control them.

24:36 Universal basic income won't fix the dignity problem
Fukuyama doesn't buy the Keynesian optimism — productivity so high that we only need to work ten to twenty hours a week and spend the rest on hobbies. He thinks that ultimately won't make people happy, and the same goes for universal basic income. The reason is thumos: megalothymia comes from this Greek word, meaning spiritedness or pride; beyond material needs, people want their basic dignity recognized. And a good part of dignity comes from what you do — being paid to do a job means someone in society thinks what you do is worth paying for. So a society where everyone sells trinkets on Etsy and no longer does the usual work won't make people happy, because it can't give them pride and a sense of accomplishment. He incidentally explains why the manosphere is so agitated: online all day, fantasizing that you're a superhero, while in reality knowing it's empty.

item.title: The thing founders should learn isn't fundraising, it's how to say no
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-howibuilt-创始人最该学的不是融资-是学会说不/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-howibuilt-创始人最该学的不是融资-是学会说不/
item.description: Beyond Yoga founder Michelle Wahler says you don't have to raise money or plan an exit — just build a business that sustains itself. Her husband stopped her from making swimwear and forced her to perfect one pair of leggings first.
item.content:encoded:
Beyond Yoga founder Michelle Wahler says you don't have to raise money or plan an exit — just build a business that sustains itself. Her husband stopped her from making swimwear and forced her to perfect one pair of leggings first.

All three callers' problems are concrete: conversion for adult study-abroad trips, a craftsman winning back old clients, a small brand selling emotion online. The answers are concrete too, not chicken soup.

4:06 You don't have to raise, and you don't have to plan an exit
Michelle says the advice entrepreneurs hear most often is ‘you have to raise’, and she thinks that's BS. Her logic: once you bring in investors, the exit becomes the company's focus and the company's trajectory changes with it. She suggests first figuring out what drives you and what you want the business to become, then building a sustainable business instead of staring at an exit. She adds: you don't have to be the next Anthropic, and you probably won't be, but there is nothing wrong with a smaller business that supports you and gives you freedom in your life.

9:17 Screen people first, then let them book a call
Carrie's adult study-abroad courses average $6,200. Plenty of people express interest, open the emails, book calls, but they just don't enroll — deadlines and discounts don't help. Michelle's suggestion is to add a few screening questions before ‘book a call’: Are you ready for a seven-day immersive experience? Are you willing to spend money on this once-in-a-lifetime investment in yourself? Are you a lifelong learner? If every answer is an enthusiastic yes, then we'll talk. That filters out the calls that were never going to convert.

10:20 No Eiffel Tower on the site, and she loses people
Carrie explains why the website doesn't show the Eiffel Tower: the travel market is crowded, and she wants to emphasize that this is an educational experience, a community of lifelong learners, not sightseeing. Michelle pushes back: the first two images on the site are a group of people looking at a map and a group of people in a classroom, and those images could be anywhere. You should show people at a glance the thing that exists only here. Guy adds another layer: what actually stops people from hitting the enroll button is the nervousness of ‘I won't know a single person’, so sell the cohort — eight days with ten equally curious people — and put up testimonials from students like ‘I was nervous at first too, I almost didn't go.’

13:31 Go to retirement communities and sign four or five at once
Michelle offers a channel idea: partner with high-end bespoke travel agencies, or with high-end independent retirement communities. She uses her own 79-year-old mother as an example — her mother lives in an independent living community surrounded by retired people, all looking for a chance to do something exciting, but afraid to go alone. Partner with communities like that and you might get four or five people signing up together at once, which is great top of funnel. Guy also suggests counterintuitively trying print media, like the New York Review of Books or the London Review of Books — spend a thousand dollars on a small ad, and the readership is exactly people over fifty with obvious intellectual curiosity.

22:53 Fix the process first, then win back old clients one by one
Grace makes custom upholstered furniture. When she started in 2021 she was flooded with demand, promised timelines too fast, and left some interior designers embarrassed in front of their clients. Michelle says the relationships can be rebuilt, but only if you first get operations in order — if you fail to deliver a second time, the relationship is completely over. The method is to make a list and go one at a time, starting with the smallest client, learning as you go and working upward, and not contacting the second until you've won back the first. Guy calls it a ‘second first impression’: don't open by asking someone to trust you again, let them see what you're making now, and ask for a small project first.

27:02 Build buffer into your quotes and deliver early
Michelle's concrete approach for Grace: first time your own process like an assembly line to understand your real capacity, then deliberately add buffer to the delivery expectations you give designers — enough buffer, but not so much that it scares them off. That way you work toward a target of two weeks early, and if you really do finish two weeks early, you call the designer and say ‘we can deliver early, or we can hold it for you’ — that's a huge plus. And if the budget was miscalculated and you really need a few extra days, that two-week buffer catches it. Either way you win.

33:15 What the website lacks isn't design, it's story
Angel makes handmade soap with a stone hidden inside that corresponds to an emotion, paired with an affirmation. At markets everyone says it's great, but online it doesn't sell. Michelle says she opened the website and couldn't find the story — even the about page was empty when you clicked in — and that's the first thing to fix today. She also points out that every product is called a ‘self-care kit’, when it should just say rose quartz, tiger eye, with a note next to it saying whether that stone corresponds to love or energy, instead of making people click into each one. And this is a perfect gifting scenario, so the copy can extend from ‘a moment for yourself’ to ‘for someone who deserves a moment more.’

35:23 You're selling a ritual, not soap
Guy uses the Calgon ad from his childhood memories as an analogy: a woman washing her hair in a bathtub, then the scene cuts to the Caribbean. He says what Angel is really selling is that ritual — wherever you are, these five minutes of product can take you away — and that costs nothing, it only requires changing how you express things on the website and then using it to tell the story across channels. Michelle adds the conversion formula: explain the ingredients and build trust, tell the story, show the product — all three have to hold at once for the sale to happen, because this is something you put on your skin.

item.title: A Bank Holiday Isn't Inefficiency, It's a Fraud Control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
item.description: The financial system going dark on weekends and holidays looks like technological backwardness, but it's a deliberately designed control: it keeps conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at once, and that exposes internal fraud.
item.content:encoded:
The financial system going dark on weekends and holidays looks like technological backwardness, but it's a deliberately designed control: it keeps conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at once, and that exposes internal fraud.

Medium information density, with the core insight concentrated in the middle and later sections: how holidays are used as an anti-fraud control, and why a 24/7 financial system doesn't hold up logically.

3:29 Holidays are a Schelling point both sides default to
A holiday isn't an authoritative list; it's a Schelling point you and your counterparty default to for each other. Nobody questions that Christmas is a holiday in the US, so nobody has to ask. But a holiday can also be the product of explicit negotiation: one reason government payroll modernization projects keep failing is that it takes a historian doing a lot of bespoke research to determine which document governs the overtime rate for a Chicago parking enforcement officer on Good Friday. A holiday is both a fact ‘every child knows’ and a negotiable object you can litigate.

6:00 The Bank of Japan's Company Foundation Day is on no official list
The Bank of Japan is also a Japanese company, so some of its human and computer systems rest on days when most office workers are at work, because that day is the bank's own Company Foundation Day. Institutions that interact with it inherit the counterparty's company founding anniversary for certain operations. That holiday appears on no list in government publications, Bloomberg, or Google Calendar, yet it carries all the consequences of a holiday. Once you trip over it, the engineering team has to urgently redefine how the system understands global holidays — because when the system asks ‘is today a holiday’, it usually passes in a jurisdiction but not a counterparty.

10:33 Black Friday falls inside the four days money doesn't move
Black Friday is the day after Thanksgiving, Cyber Monday follows right behind, and transaction volumes on those two days spike as predictably as the sun rising — and they land exactly inside a four-day window when the banking system basically doesn't move money between companies. If you promise a customer ‘we'll pay out the next business day’ while the underlying rail takes two business days to get the money to you, you have a one-day mismatch, and that mismatch consumes float. Normally you only have to front one day, three days over a weekend, and around five days during BFCM, which includes the biggest sales day of the year. That's why several hundred people spend weeks ahead of time walking through BFCM scenarios, writing contingency plans, and modeling float requirements with finance.

21:29 Crypto tried 24/7, and two banks closing at once broke it
Heavily online technologists hate systems that go down on a predictable schedule, and the crypto crowd especially loves always-on distributed systems with no single point of failure. One idea is to have every market participant bank at the same bank, get internal APIs for book transfers, and money can flow 24/7, with a second bank for redundancy. Crypto did try this path, and then in 2023 discovered just how questionable the design was when two highly correlated banks closed on adjacent weekends at the same time. The lesson: systems that mediate between cultures are useful, and mediating systems often need to bridge gaps in operating schedules, and that gap can't be eliminated by declaring ‘the only operating schedule is 24/7’.

23:30 Forced vacation is about keeping conspirators from assembling
Banks deliberately create misaligned operating schedules; it's an important tool for detecting and containing certain kinds of fraud. The most terrifying fraud comes from insiders who know the back-office processes: a single insider who understands the back office is enough to bring down a bank or cause billions in losses — Barings and Daiwa in '95, Société Générale in '08, UBS in '11 are all examples. A very old control is forced vacation, and its purpose is to keep the group involved in a conspiracy from assembling enough co-conspirators, in the right place on the right day, all sitting at the keyboard at once. So a financial CEO sleeping on a beanbag chair in the office may be very dedicated, but both the company and he himself had better not allow it.

26:31 Expecting the financial system to be always-on isn't even self-consistent
In a world that's increasingly interconnected, where decision-makers increasingly care about nines, it's reasonable to expect the financial system to partially narrow the gap between historical practice and contemporary practice. Culture creates systems, and systems create culture; both change, and infrastructure changes far more slowly than fashion, but it does change. Still, expecting the financial system to run continuously isn't just something you shouldn't expect — it isn't even a self-consistent expectation: the financial system is an interconnected network of organizations, systems, and subsystems nested layer upon layer, and at the bottom it depends on individuals who have been made complex sociocultural promises and who have a physiological need for sleep. These people will keep resting and celebrating periodically, just as they keep working for the society the financial system supports.

item.title: The Houthis seize a second strait, and $100 oil is just the start
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/
item.description: Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered. Now the Houthis have taken Barim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, and Saudi Arabia's alternate export route around Hormuz is in doubt too.
item.content:encoded:
Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered. Now the Houthis have taken Barim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, and Saudi Arabia's alternate export route around Hormuz is in doubt too.

Eight minutes to explain why a strait most people have never heard of suddenly matters, with concrete mechanics and numbers. Good for a commute.

2:00 The Red Sea is not just another waterway
In normal, calm times, nearly 15% of global seaborne trade passes through the Red Sea, including 30% of global container shipping, 12% of seaborne oil trade and 8% of liquefied natural gas. At its northern end the Red Sea connects to Egypt and the Suez Canal, and on to the Mediterranean; at its southern end that narrow channel leading to the Indian Ocean and Asian trade routes is the Bab-el-Mandeb. To grasp the weight of this strait, you first have to grasp how much the Red Sea itself carries — it is not a bypass you can casually route around, but a stretch of the global trade artery.

3:05 The Houthis really did take that ground
The host pressed Rachel on whether "seem to have seized" was hedging, and Rachel confirmed it: the Houthis are a rebel group that has gradually taken control of large parts of Yemen since at least 2014, allied with Iran, and strongly opposed to Israel's existence and to how Israel is fighting in Gaza. In November 2023 they began attacking Red Sea shipping, hijacking vessels and striking with drones and missiles; the US military responded with bombing, and the Red Sea was relatively calm for a while. But over the weekend they moved, seizing a stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast, possibly to support Iran.

4:09 Barim Island is the key that pinches the strait
The seized stretch includes an island right in the middle of the Bab-el-Mandeb — Barim Island, which the military calls "key terrain" because it overlooks the entire strait, and the strait is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point. Whoever controls that chokepoint decides which ships can pass. Red Sea traffic had already slowed because of the Houthi attacks, initially falling 50%, and it never fully recovered. Now that Barim Island has been taken, the threat is that this route shuts down entirely.

4:09 Saudi Arabia's way around Hormuz is in doubt too
This is especially thorny for Saudi Arabia. After Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz more than six months ago, Saudi Arabia had been treating the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb as an alternative oil export route, sending oil through an east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports and loading it there. But last week that Saudi Red Sea pipeline was hit by a drone attack, and Saudi Arabia then suspended oil loadings from one Red Sea port. Rachel says this puts more pressure on this lifeline for Saudi Arabia and for the global economy — the creative workaround meant to buffer the world economy is itself extremely fragile.

5:10 Schrodinger Strait: you can collect tolls without firing a shot
The Houthis could close the Bab-el-Mandeb at any time, but so far they haven't. Rachel says the mere fact that they can is already having an effect. Analysts call it the "Schrodinger Strait" — is it open or closed? That uncertainty alone pushes up insurance costs and freight rates and adds friction to the global economy. After news of the Houthi advance last week, oil prices spiked above $100 a barrel.

6:10 Refined products are rising more sharply than crude
Rachel points out that timing is crucial: a global supply gap was already building, only partly offset by rerouting and releases from strategic petroleum reserves, and refineries have seen severe outages. That means not only is crude more expensive, but diesel, gasoline and other petroleum products are rising by proportionally more, because getting refined products to market has become harder. It isn't just oil products — this strait also carries fertilizer and natural gas, which would be a problem if Europe has a cold winter.

7:10 Sulfur and helium: the overlooked knock-on shortages
Sulfur is a byproduct of natural gas and fuel production, its supply is already more constrained, and it is used in metal processing, including copper. Helium is a byproduct of natural gas deposits, used as an input in semiconductors and in all kinds of medical equipment. Countries including the US and Canada are ramping up production of some of these goods, offsetting part of the price increase, but Rachel says not by much. That means shortages from this new trade disruption will reach ordinary people before long.

7:10 American consumers end up footing the bill
Rachel says Americans should care because these are global markets, and you can't build a wall and stop importing. Some US producers may benefit from shortages, but in this scenario American consumers tend to be the ones who lose. She also warns that it isn't just higher prices to worry about: the Houthi actions, plus Iran's refusal to yield, are straining relations among regional countries and between the US and its Middle East allies. Deteriorating US relations with its allies could make other US policy goals harder to achieve — Gulf states, for instance, are major investors in the US and key to US onshore production.

item.title: The bottleneck in voice AI isn't the model, it's a 150-millisecond biological constraint
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-twiml-语音-ai-的瓶颈不是模型-是-150-毫秒的生物学约束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-twiml-语音-ai-的瓶颈不是模型-是-150-毫秒的生物学约束/
item.description: Human audiovisual perception runs at only 6-10 hertz, and the model has to be interruptible inside that window; meanwhile high-fidelity audio means more tokens per second, and more tokens means fewer parameters — this is the physical trade-off voice AI cannot avoid.
item.content:encoded:
Human audiovisual perception runs at only 6-10 hertz, and the model has to be interruptible inside that window; meanwhile high-fidelity audio means more tokens per second, and more tokens means fewer parameters — this is the physical trade-off voice AI cannot avoid.

The first half is hands-on product and architecture judgment; the second half, on EQ, benchmarks and the personalization learning loop, is worth more, but you have to be patient and listen past the 45-minute mark.

6:09 150 milliseconds is a hard constraint, not an engineering tuning knob
Alex's starting point is biology: from a photon hitting the retina to the cortex responding takes about 150 milliseconds, and that number is stable enough to serve as a non-invasive diagnostic marker for neurodegenerative disease — when there is pathology the signal takes a detour and takes longer. Human audiovisual perception actually runs at 6 to 10 hertz, even though the world feels perfectly smooth to us. So their model handles interruptions inside a window of roughly 150 milliseconds. This is not an engineering goal of ‘as fast as possible’, it is a hard design input aligned to the human perceptual frame rate.

8:11 Token rate and parameter count are zero-sum
Audio first has to be turned into tokens and fed into the LLM backbone, then turned back into audio. High fidelity requires a high token rate, but a high token rate means prefilling and generating a large number of tokens every second, and the cost rises accordingly. That produces an unpleasant dilemma: more tokens per second means the model parameters cannot be too large; fewer tokens per second is what lets you afford more parameters. Text is the ultimate compression format, needing only 3 to 5 tokens per second, while audio easily goes above 10. 10 tokens/second means each token covers about 100 milliseconds — which is why user-experience engineering and scientific research have to be done at the same time.

11:14 Most avatar video is boring, so it compresses
Models like WAN and Flux can generate video clips of around 10 seconds, but producing an hour of visually consistent continuous stream requires changing the model. Alex's key insight is: if you know this is avatar video, there won't be race cars flying through the background, and most of the frame is fairly boring. So the audiovisual stream of this interview can be compressed into a quite efficient bitstream; the bitrate only spikes when he waves his arms wildly, and normal people don't do that. This is the concrete landing point of ‘set the price first, then work backwards to the architecture’ — not chasing the prettiest picture quality, but building something users can afford.

15:17 Teach a model a new modality and it forgets its old skills
They didn't build their own LLM; instead they took the intelligence already present in a high-quality LLM and had it learn one more modality. But the risk is catastrophic forgetting. Alex gives the example of a friend: he adopted a Latin American child in Germany and spoke only German to her, and within a few months the girl had forgotten all her Spanish words. LLMs are the same — let one handle only audio and it will soon forget reasoning and language itself. So you have to maintain a competitive mid/post-training LLM pipeline, and at the same time define tasks that graft audio and text together, just as a multilingual model has to know that dog and Hund refer to the same thing.

20:24 100 million hours of audio — only a self-built data center can afford to store it
Their training data is on the order of 100 million hours of audio, which Alex converts into roughly 200 human lifetimes — if you lived 75 years and were always in a noisy environment, that is about how much audio you would hear. This data can be crawled from the web, but it needs extraction, labeling, normalization and transcription, a great deal of extra processing. Building their own data center helped enormously here: putting it on NeoCloud would eat you alive in storage bills, and putting it on the big three cloud providers is even worse. He also mentions a timing point: hard drive prices are now about three times what they were last year, so they will have to be frugal going forward.

23:28 Squeeze labels out of noise with medieval statistics
Faced with noisy labels produced by imperfect processing tools, Alex's argument is: as long as the noise is unbiased, averaging a large number of repeated measurements gives a better estimate than any single one. He cites the medieval ‘foot’ — have people walk out of the church, take the first 12 men, remove the two with the longest feet and the two with the shortest (possibly because of deformities), average the remaining 8, and you get an estimate of one foot. He says robust regression and estimation have existed for half a millennium. Concretely for audio: knowing this is a two-person podcast, knowing TWIML is usually Sam plus one other person, makes it easy to separate speakers, obtain a large amount of single-speaker audio, and thereby label better, forming a flywheel.

33:43 End-to-end audio models are doomed to be small and dumb
Alex is very blunt about the architecture choice: end-to-end audio models have their place — fast response, small footprint, low latency — but they are also fairly dumb. Make them smart and the compute cost becomes unbearable. So their approach is two-stage: understanding and reasoning happen at one end, the backend triggers the appropriate tool calls, and then the answer is collected back, like multithreaded programming where the main thread dispatches parallel threads and retrieves the results. For the user, writing a prompt for their model looks the same as writing a prompt for an ordinary LLM, except their model also talks.

36:46 Ten times cheaper than GPT, but with thinking turned off
Alex claims that on benchmarks like BigBench Audio and Complex Function Bench they beat GPT, Gemini and Grok, at one tenth the cost of OpenAI's models. But he adds a footnote himself: this was measured with thinking turned off. The reason is that you cannot let the model pause to think before answering — that feels very unnatural, and humans don't do it either. This exposes a fundamental constraint of the voice setting — reasoning ability has to be hidden in the background, and there can be no visible thinking pause in the foreground.

item.title: Clovis people didn't just hunt mammoths — they painted and sewed inside tents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
item.description: Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles have been excavated at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA and protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the label "mammoth hunter" suggests.
item.content:encoded:
Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles have been excavated at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA and protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the label "mammoth hunter" suggests.

The archaeological detail is dense but demands patience: the first half is Clovis research history and dating debates, and the concrete findings at LaPrele in the second half are the part that's really worth it.

3:02 Clovis lasted only a few hundred years
Radiocarbon dating pins Clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago, a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the Ice Age. The narrowness of that span is itself startling — the Ice Age is a scale of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and Clovis is only an instant within it. More crucially, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone spear points appeared across the entire North American continent, from New Mexico to Wyoming, from Washington State to Virginia. This combination of "narrow in time, wide in space" is Clovis's most distinctive feature; in later periods, spear points rapidly regionalized.

12:21 Clovis were not the first Americans
The "Clovis First" theory dominated most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the Americas, and Clovis people were the earliest settlers. But discoveries at sites such as Monte Verde (Chile), Paisley Caves (Oregon), Cooper's Ferry (Idaho) and Page-Ladson (Florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe that people were living in the Americas thousands of years before Clovis. Mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in American archaeology, and Pleistocene archaeologists have argued hard over it. But she also stresses that Clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves.

21:01 One chopper changed the nature of the whole site
The LaPrele site was discovered in 1986 when locals found mammoth bones by a creek, and Mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. In the first season, retired archaeologist Rich Adams, while helping everyone repair the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. The key point is that it appeared in a position where it geologically should not have been: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved such a large cobble there. This tool prompted the team to test a wider area, ultimately revealing more than 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, several hundred stone tools and mammoth ivory. LaPrele was no longer just a kill site but a camp where humans had lived.

29:15 Hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment
LaPrele's most striking find is four "hearth-centered areas." In the Block B area, the team found no obvious ash or oxidation traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small patch, indicating a hearth once stood there. Even more compelling is the spatial analysis: if you look down from above at a tent, the hearth is at the center, surrounded by an area of intensive activity, then an open space for walking, and near the tent wall objects accumulate — because the wall is a barrier to the movement of artifacts. The artifact distribution in Block B shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an indoor space. In the same area, a scatter of ochre (hematite) pigment about 1.5 meters by 2 meters was found, matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire.

39:25 The bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone
The team used ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; this method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. The results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox, and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. Mackey notes that these animals are all fur-bearing, and their bone thickness may have been just right for making needles. More importantly, these animals were likely caught in traps rather than hunted with spears. This means Clovis people were not hunting mammoths 24 hours a day; they were also taking more common small prey.

44:32 Were Clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores?
About 15 widely accepted Clovis sites in North America are associated with megafauna, mostly proboscideans (mammoths, mastodons, gomphotheres), but also horses and camels. Yet Mackey points out that only about 30 to 40 sites truly define our understanding of Clovis, while thousands of Clovis spear points have been found on the surface, lacking context. This raises a core debate: were they mammoth-hunting specialists, or omnivores with a broader diet? Small animals, fish and plant remains preserve less well and are less often systematically sought. Mackey is studying plant remains, and she notes that archaeologists usually look for plants only in hearths, and how many places in the Clovis record have actually been looked at is a problem.

50:00 Mammoth extinction: did humans give a push, or was climate the main driver?
The classic "overkill" debate: 35 genera of megafauna went extinct at the end of the Ice Age — how much was due to human factors and how much to environmental factors? Mackey says she takes a middle path, believing both contributed. She considers mammoths the strongest candidate for the overkill hypothesis, because mammoth sites are numerous, the animals were large, and their reproductive rate was low, making them more vulnerable to hunting. But she also notes that overkill doesn't necessarily mean humans hunted all 35 genera; rather, hunting may have upset the balance through trophic cascades. Interestingly, the paleoecology community leans toward "humans did it," while the archaeology community leans more toward "the environment did it."

53:12 Clovis human bone barely exists
Apart from a single ancestral burial attributed to Clovis at the Anzick site in Montana, we have almost no Clovis human bone.
